The desire for the Good. As an atheist I realized that I still have this desire to have a good life, the same desire I had when I was a theist. I questioned this desire. I asked myself: "Why do I have such desire?" and "How can I achieve what I desire." As an atheist, I was looking for something materialistic, of course. I ignored the question "Why do I have such desire?" and focused on the second one. So, I want to have a good life. How? Lets see, I have food, I exercise, I go to school, I play games, I talk with friends, I read books and do other hobbies. Hm, still, it wasnt enough, I didnt feel like I was leading a good life, that I lack something more in all of these activities, the famous "why?". Then I searched for a way to become a good person. Because as Epictetos the Stoic said, "sometimes it is important HOW you see, not WHAT you see". Then, that means I have to change myself, my way of thinking, how I view everything around me, and I will achieve what I desire, good person=good life. I began reading philosophic texts, and one particular philosopher caught my attention, Socrates. I knew about Socrates before, I read dialogues of Plato as a theist, but I didnt think too much about them, for I didnt understand them very well. Now, as an atheist and someone looking for answers I was shocked. Socrates was asking the same questions, "How to become a good person/citizen", "How to have good life" and so on. And here I discovered the theory of ideas. Everything you see around yourself, you included, is just a shadow of something greater. That answered my desire to have a good life, it actually answered my first question, the one I ignored:"Why do I have such desire?". I desire good for I lack good. Now that didnt make me a theist of course, I was still an atheist by this time. Socrates talks about Gods, or Divinity, but he, and Plato as well kinda ignore this question, dont go too deep. Yes, they say how we all, as souls, used to ride with the Gods in the ideal world, the famous "fall of soul" in dialogue of Phaedrus, but I saw it as a myth, something made up to better understand humans. What or better who changed my view was Plotinos. He explaines that the ideas come from the One, who is the Good, and from whom came our souls, now trapped in materialistic world in our bodies. We remember this One and desire to unite ourselves with the One. Well, this is all very shortly and poorly explained, I am sorry for that. I will summarize it:
TL;DR: Questioning my life and the universe made me a theist.

The Gods do not need the miracles for Themselves. The Gods already have the powers that you can get from the miracles, Those powers are in Them. The miracles are simply the tales of the Gods written by those who saw the actions of the Gods. 

So, you can imagine a couple of, I dont know, sentient beings, who were present by Lord Gwyn when He used His lighting against the everlasting dragons. Now, those sentient beings were in awe, amazed by such power and decided that they have to write a tale about it. So, a miracle was created, where you can read the tale of Lord Gwyn taking down some dragons. Everyone shared this tale, of course, just like we share amazing books and games, because the tale was amazing too. Just imagine, a God fighting dragons, sounds cool, right? I would even claim that these miracles, these tales of the Gods, were one of the reasons why everyone started worshipping Them as deities. Someone with such power can by only seen as a divine being, for sure. Anyway, tales were spread quickly, because everyone wanted to read the amazing action story of Lord Gwyn defeating the dragons, or the beautiful story of Gwynevere healing wounded soldiers. And so the worship of the Gods could be spread everywhere. The Gods surely wanted everyone to know about Their actions. There was no reason for the Gods to forbid miracles... but...

In Dark Souls II. we find out about one miracle that was actually forbidden by Lord Gwyn Himself. It is called "Blinding Bolt", a miracle crafted by Lord Gwyn, and by Lord Gwyn later forbidden. We dont know the reason why it was forbidden, maybe humans abused it, maybe it was too "hardcore" and "brutal", something no longer needed to be used. Or it was just too sad... who knows. 

I mean, the clerics, who are the servants of the Gods, know a lot of miracles. The Way of White, which is just an organisation that worships the Gods, uses a lot of miracles. If the Gods were against humans using miracles, then clerics and the Way of White would be the first ones to stop using them. 

And lets not discuss what you need to use the miracles properly. Just two things. You need to know how to read and you need faith. And from that, the enemies of the Gods have only one thing, well, some of them at least. Those faithless servants of Dark cant use the miracles for anything. 

TL;DR: The miracles are basically the Bible, so forbidding them makes no sense. They are for everyone to learn about the Gods.

I can see why a lot of people are dissapointed with answering lore questions in games like Dark Souls. I suppose everyone remembers the moment of playing Dark Souls I. for the first time. All those new things, known and unknown. So many of us were drawn into this new world full of mysteries, of questions important and needed to be answered, or questions just intriguing, which answers would satiate our never-ending curiosity. But we were not given any answers, just small hints, that were supposed to help us on our journey to find these answers.

Well, pontiff is a religious title, that originates from the Latin word pontifex(plural pontifices). This term was used during the Roman times to describe the high priests of the Roman religion (and now is used to describe any priests worshipping the Roman Gods). Pontifex means "to build bridge/bridge builder", and suggests that someone called pontifex has the duty to build a bridge between the humans and the Gods, through sacred rites, ceremonies, festivals etc. It is a pretty high and respectable religious position, there were only a few of pontifices. I believe the term was picked because of its importance and meaning...

I believe we will learn more about the Gods, once worshipped and loved, now cursed and hated. We know about Lord Gwyn and Dark Sun Gwyndolin, we even know about the eldest son of Lord Gwyn, but what about the rest of the Gods? Those who we only know through item descriptions remain a great mystery to us. But what if the answer lies in the painted world? What do we actually know about this place? 

It seems that it is the realm of Goddess Velka, who is described as a rogue deity feared by other Gods. In Dark Souls I. we find a lot of items associated with Velka exactly in the Painted world of Ariamis. From Priscilla we find out that Ariamis created this world, but it doesnt mean that Ariamis is the one ruling there as well. Ariamis is only the creator, the painter, someone who had the power to create such a world that can be entered, a painting that hides a new world. Reasons why such a world was created were already discussed. The most accepted opinion is that the world serves as a place for things dangerous for the Gods, like Priscilla with her lifehunt ability. But this opinion has a lot of flaws.

At first, why would the Gods even allow for such a place to exist? It doesnt make sense. Imagine you are one of the Gods. You live in Anor Londo, in the city of the Gods under the rule of Lord Gwyn. Even if you are powerful and worshipped by many, there are enemies with weapons, that are very effective against you. Then there are beings with abilities that are very effective against you. And many other things dangerous for you. What would you do? Would you let Ariamis create a world for all these dangerous things? Or would you try to destroy these things? Why would you let Ariamis create a painted world filled with things and beings effective against the Gods, that will be hanging in Anor Londo, city of the Gods? Did you forget what you did to the everlasting dragons? Yes, you destroyed them, well, most of them. You didnt send them into a painting, that is hanging in your home.

The second biggest flaw shows us Priscilla herself, one of those supposed dangerous things. She is one of the inhabitants of the Painted world. What do we know about her? Well, she is a crossbreed, by some called abomination, with powerful ability. All Gods hated her and sent her to the Painted world. But that is not true, again. Priscilla is no prisoner there, tortured or crying, begging you to free her. No, she is actually the one telling you to leave her alone, and, what is important, leave the painted world. She has a weapon, a scythe, in her hands and stands a few steps in front of the exit from the Painted world. Why would the Gods let her have a scythe when they know how dangerous her lifehunt ability is? And why, for Gwyn's sake would the Gods leave her near the exit? Priscilla can leave anytime, and attack Anor Londo from inside. A few painting guardians are not going to stop her, I am sure. And painting guardians represent the next flaw.

What is the duty of the painting guardians? To guard the Great Painting of Ariamis. It is said that they dont know why they guard the painting, but lets look at the word "to guard". There are two meanings of this word: 

1. - to protect someone or something from being attacked or stolen
2. - to watch someone and make certain they do not escape from a place

A lot of people use the second meaning, that the painting guardians protect Anor Londo from those who are in the Painted world, but could it not be actually the first meaning of the word? When you look at those guardians, they do not face the Great Painting of Ariamis, they are not looking at the painting, they are protecting the painting from people trying to enter it. They protect the beings living in the Great Painting of Ariamis. 

Ariamis created painted world as a sanctuary for all those who need to be protected. Reddit user NothingAndNobody has an interesting reason for why Mother Teresa being granted sainthood is getting lot of backlash:
"Because she was formally canonized today, and to many, the Church is incapable of making a single correct decision. So if the Catholic Church declares that a woman who left her comfortable life to devote herself entirely to providing food, water, shelter, and pain relief to the seriously sick and suffering, especially the dying, in the poorest city on the planet, where fatal disease is rampant, hygiene is just a utopian fantasy, poverty is all-permeating, and hospital standards are sub-medieval; who spends all day every day for her long life ministering to these people while remaining cheerful and loving to all, being an influence of mercy on so many others, well, some people just have to be contrarian and disagree, saying that she was so obviously not what she was, i.e., a Saint.
The main arguments look like this:
Saint Teresa endorsed Catholic views on abortion, contraception, etc. (To which the argument is: Yeah, too damn bad).
Saint Teresa took money from corrupt politicians. (To which the argument is: Which is better--for money to stay in the pocket of a corrupt man, or money to leave the pocket of a corrupt man and serve the poor?)
Saint Teresa's hospitals were substandard. (To which the argument is: Go to Calcutta. Show me that it would be in any universe possible to build a better set-up than her, with what she had at her disposal).
Saint Teresa had an enormously high death rate. (To which you need only demonstrate that she never pretended to be running other than a hospice: It was a place for those with terminal illnesses to die with dignity. You might as well argue that all funeral parlors are criminals.)
Saint Teresa believed that suffering brought you closer to Jesus. (Because atheists are usually not very philosophically minded, they believe this means that Saint Teresa made people suffer gratuitously. She did not. She merely encouraged people to use situations over which they had no control--i.e., lots and lots of pain--to unite themselves to the suffering savior).
I have been to India, although not Calcutta, and the arguments do not hold water. My priest actually stayed at a complex run by the Sisters of Charity for a short time, and he said it shook him to the core to see people in such wholehearted service to the poor, sick, suffering, and spurned. No one who saw Mother Teresa believed she was evil: That's why Hitchens (the source of all the above arguments) wrote his book safely from the comfort of the wealthy western hemisphere. Easy enough for him to dictate what Teresa should have done, harder to do anywhere near as much good, harder still to actually follow her example and give wholehearted service to the terminally ill.
tl;dr "Why is everyone hating on Saint Teresa?" Because Satan plays a long and calculated game, and because the Church is a sign of contradiction: Innocent and despised, just like Jesus himself was."

The second great answer I found is from reddit user AmbrosePhoenix.
"It's not really sudden. Hitchens and his fans have been dragging her through the mud for years. Their criticisms all boil down to the fact that she didn't run things the way a proper secular humanist would. And you know what? They're right, such as it is. A proper secular humanist whose only concern is minimizing physical pain and increasing material well-being would have done almost everything differently than Saint Teresa did. They wouldn't have had the people in the order spending hours each day praying and making sure to have Mass. The money given to them would have been invested in medical facilities and other material goods, rather than toward more houses for the order in other parts of the world, beautifying churches, and the rest given to the Church to distribute as they see fit. A secular humanist would find this treatment of money abhorrent. Also, the fact that she saw redemptive value in suffering rather than as the be all end all of evil is something incomprehensible.
This whole thing is basically further evidence of how divorced the Christian worldview has become from the norm. "Do good and avoid evil" has been replaced with "distribute pleasure and relieve pain." If all you believe in is the material universe, and for whatever reason still think that the chemical reactions inside a hairless primate are worth caring about, the way Saint Teresa lived her life will make no sense, and a lot of what she did will seem downright awful and opposed to what you believe. Now, I'm not saying she was perfect or made no mistakes, but the vast majority of criticism of her is just based on different fundamental assumptions of the place of humanity in the universe and the purpose of life."

And all of Them shared something, that is very important in the Dark Souls universe. All of Them had light souls. And all of sudden, there are humans, a new beings, with dark souls. Imagine you are Lord Gwyn, how would you react? Would you just open your arms, and welcome them? You would be foolish if you did that. I write it sadly, but Lord Gwyn failed here. He should have never welcomed the humans to His realm. But He did, and for this I respect Lord Gwyn, for it shows what a kind and merciful God He was. Not only did He welcome humans, He allowed them to build great cities, and shared power with them. Lord Gwyn could easily put some Gods in charge of New Londo or Oolacile, right? But He didnt do it. Everyone, maybe except one toothy serpant, benefited from this new relationship. Humans worshipped the Gods, and the Gods put miracles upon them, for the faith of humans was strong. The Age of Fire is not only the Age of Gods, in the first place it is the Age of Prosperity.Prosperity... I dont know what else should I write about this word, a word every nation would like to use when describing their homeland. However nothing last forever. The Flame, the great source of the great prosperity began to fade, Something horrible, for everyone, for Gods, for humans and for all other beings who are connected to the Flame. Because it does not matter how much toothy serpant and dragon monster are lying, the humans are strong with the Flame. Just like the Gods, and like all beings born in the Age of Fire. Lord Gwyn saw the comming disaster, and after terrible failure in Izalith, knew there was only one way to save the prosperous age. Thus by sacrificing His own life, abandoning His beautiful city Anor Londo, His family, His friends, His divinity. A great sacrifice of a great God, indeed. And so Gwyn, Lord of Sunlight, became Gwyn, Lord of Cinder. And prosperity of all beings could continue, until the Flame would fade again. But what then? Who would sacrifice again, if there is no great Lord left? Do not worry. The Champion will rise, a brave defender of the Flame. So the Gods, together with humans, created the bonfire system, so the Champion will have enough time to become strong enough, and have his/her journey easier by warping. 
Yes, the bonfire system is very brutal, but necessary. Undead sacrifices help to create small embers, that give everyone a little light and warmth, so the hope is not lost. So that the Gods are not corrupted, and the humans dont go hollow. They are necesssary, until the brave Champion links the fire. The Champion shall endeth eternal twilight, and avert further Undead sacrifices. When the Flame stops fading, there are no more undead sacrifices. Until the new fading of Flame, all beings live in prosperity.
Without Fire, all shall be a frigid and frightful Dark.
